title: Test-driven development
idea: Test-driven development (TDD) lets tests drive the design: you write one failing test, make it pass with the least code, then clean up.
points: Red: write one small test for the next behaviour and watch it fail.
Green: write the simplest code that passes, even if it looks naive.
Refactor: rename, extract and remove duplication while every test stays green.
Tests written first force a small public API that is easy to call.

hero.title: Three turns of the late-fee cycle

steps.caption: Pick the next behaviour from the list: a book three days late costs 75 cents.
Write the test first. `cents(3)` still returns 0, so the run shows FAIL.
Add the least code that passes: past two grace days, 25 cents per late day. Every test now prints PASS.
Refactor: replace the magic numbers with `GRACE_DAYS` and `CENTS_PER_DAY`. Run tests again.
Back to the list. Cap tests at 19 and 20 days go red, then green, and the cycle repeats.
A test for 90 million days goes red: the `int` multiply overflowed. Using `long` turns it green.

code.title: Red
code.caption: The third test is written before the code. The failure names the next job.

walk.text: Two earlier cycles needed only `return 0`. TDD forbids writing more than tests demand.
The new test states the rule as an example: three days late costs 75 cents.
JUnit is not here, so a tiny `check` runner prints PASS or FAIL and collects failures.
The summary shows exactly one failing test. One red test means one clear next step.

code.title: After many cycles
code.caption: Eight tests, each added red first. The code is small because nothing untested was written.

walk.text: Boundary tests at 19 and 20 days pin exactly where the cap starts.
This test failed with `int` arithmetic: the product wrapped negative, so the fee went negative.
Bad input is a behaviour too. The test demands an `IllegalArgumentException`.
Refactor steps named the rules. Tests stayed green after each rename.
Multiplying as `long` before the cap is the fix the overflow test forced.

pitfalls: Writing five tests before any code; you lose the single red signal that guides you.
Skipping the refactor step; green but messy code piles up quickly.
Never seeing a new test fail; it may pass by accident and test nothing.

quiz.q: Your new test passes the first time you run it, before any code change. What should you do?
options: Commit it; a passing test is the goal
Make it fail first to prove it tests something
Delete the production code and start the cycle again
Write the next three tests before checking anything
quiz.why: A test that was never red may test nothing, or the behaviour already exists. Break the code briefly or sharpen the test so you see it fail.

takeaway: Red, green, refactor: one failing test at a time drives the design.

starters: How would I test-drive a class that needs a repository?
Should I use TDD in an LLD interview?
